passage: Tuesday night. Pankaj laughed at Rohit's joke about the tea seller today. Last year he walked out of a room when someone did that. Everyone laughed: Tanya, Rohit, the two new boys from Pankaj's lab group. I did not, and Tanya looked at me, then looked away. Pankaj caught my eye and stopped laughing a second too late. I do not want to say anything in front of everyone. Tomorrow I will ask him for chai, just us, and say what I noticed, not that he is wrong. Maybe there is a reason. Maybe I am the one who has it wrong. — Shalini

qa.q: Whose joke did Pankaj laugh at?
qa.a: Pankaj laughed at Rohit's joke about the tea seller.

qa.q: What is Shalini worried about, and why does Shalini hold back from speaking in front of everyone?
qa.a: Shalini is worried and unsure: a change in Pankaj was noticed, but Shalini does not want to confront anyone publicly and allows that there may be a reason.

qa.q: What choice does Shalini make about how to raise the change with Pankaj?
qa.a: Shalini plans a private chai with Pankaj, saying what was noticed rather than saying Pankaj is wrong, which leaves room for an explanation.

qa.q: What might Pankaj be feeling when catching Shalini's eye and stopping the laugh a second too late?
qa.a: Pankaj may feel caught between fitting in and old values; stopping late suggests discomfort or guilt at what everyone was laughing at.

grounding: A person notices someone laughing at jokes they used to dislike and chooses a private, kind check-in over public teasing.

passage:
Varun had known Rekha since the bus rides to the kasba college. She was the one who used to shut down the jokes about Guddu's English.
Now, at the tea stall after exams, Mohan did Guddu's accent again and Rekha laughed loudest, slapping the bench.
“Since when are you in the comedy club, madam?” Sonu shouted, and the whole group hooted. Rekha's smile froze.
Varun said nothing then. On the evening bus home, when the others had got down at the mandi stop, he asked quietly, “You okay? You used to hate those jokes.”
Rekha looked at the dusty window for a long time. “My new hostel friends laugh at everything like that. I didn't want to be the boring one.” She sighed. “I don't even find it funny.”

qa.q: Where did the group meet after exams?
qa.a: They met at the tea stall after exams.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when Rekha laughed at the jokes?
qa.a: He felt surprised and uneasy, since she used to shut those jokes down, but he stayed quiet in front of the group.

qa.q: Why was Varun's timing a good choice?
qa.a: He waited until the others had got off and asked privately and gently, so Rekha could explain without being laughed at again.

qa.q: How did Sonu's public shout affect Rekha?
qa.a: It embarrassed her; her smile froze, and it gave her no room to explain why she was acting differently.

grounding: A friend notices someone laughing at jokes she used to dislike and checks in privately, which lets her explain, unlike the public teasing.

passage:
Ulla first noticed at the shared flat dinner in Aarhus. Mateo, who had been vegetarian since school, took a big piece of pork and joked, “Plants have feelings too.” The new flatmates, Sven and Katrine, laughed and clinked glasses with him.
“Wow, Mateo the carnivore!” Katrine said, and Sven started a slow clap.
Mateo laughed too, but he chewed slowly and drank a lot of water.
The next morning Ulla found him alone in the kitchen. She made two coffees and said, “Hey. No judgement. Last night looked like hard work. Did you change your mind about meat, or something else?”
Mateo rubbed his eyes. “I just wanted them to stop calling me the fussy one.” He paused. “I'm not sure what I want yet.”

qa.q: Who were the new flatmates?
qa.a: Sven and Katrine were the new flatmates.

qa.q: What was Ulla thinking when she said last night looked like hard work?
qa.a: She felt concerned and caring; she had noticed Mateo chewing slowly and drinking lots of water and suspected he was forcing himself.

qa.q: How could Ulla keep supporting Mateo from here?
qa.a: She could leave the choice to him, avoid bringing it up at group dinners, and make it easy for him to cook vegetarian with her if he wants.

qa.q: What might the slow clap have felt like for Mateo?
qa.a: It probably felt like pressure and a spotlight, rewarding him for dropping a value he wasn't sure he wanted to drop.

grounding: A friend notices someone dropping a long-held value around new people and chooses a private, kind check-in instead of teasing.

passage:
Every Sunday for two years, Madhuri had taught the watchmen's children in the college's literacy room. Tenzin noticed when she stopped coming.
At the hostel mess, Madhuri's new friends were joking about “social service types who want medals.” Madhuri laughed along. Pema, at the next table, called out, “Arre, look who's joined the cool gang!” Heads turned. Madhuri stared at her plate.
Tenzin waited. That night she knocked on Madhuri's door with two packets of biscuits. “I'm not here to lecture. The kids asked about you. Is everything alright?”
Madhuri sat on her bed. “I'm so tired this semester. And when they joked, it was easier to laugh than explain.” She picked at the biscuit wrapper. “Maybe I'll come next Sunday. Maybe.”

qa.q: What did Madhuri do every Sunday for two years?
qa.a: She taught the watchmen's children in the college's literacy room.

qa.q: How was Tenzin feeling when she knocked on Madhuri's door?
qa.a: She felt concerned but careful; she brought biscuits and promised no lecture because she wanted Madhuri to feel safe to talk.

qa.q: What did Tenzin's approach do better than Pema's?
qa.a: Tenzin asked privately and kindly, leaving space for an answer, while Pema's shout in the mess only made Madhuri stare at her plate.

qa.q: What was it like for Madhuri when heads turned in the mess?
qa.a: She likely felt embarrassed and cornered, caught between her new friends and the person she used to be.

grounding: A friend notices someone dropping a long-held commitment and laughing at it, and a private, kind check-in lets her explain.

passage:
Siddharth,
I'm writing this instead of saying it in the mess, because I don't want an audience.
Last night at Rohan's birthday, Kunal did that joke about the canteen uncle's accent. Everyone laughed, and so did you. In first year you were the one who walked out when someone mocked how the laundry aunty spoke. You told me that kind of joke made your skin crawl.
Maybe you've changed your mind, and that's allowed. Maybe you're just tired of being the odd one out in the new group. I saw the others glance at you, and Kunal started on "Siddharth's new sense of humour." I didn't join in, and I won't.
If something's going on, I'd like to hear it, over chai at the gate stall, whenever you want. If nothing is, tell me I'm overthinking and I'll drop it.
Still your friend,
Harish

qa.q: Where does Harish suggest meeting Siddharth to talk?
qa.a: Over chai at the gate stall, whenever Siddharth wants.

qa.q: What is Harish feeling while writing this letter?
qa.a: Harish seems uneasy and a little sad to see Siddharth laugh at a joke Siddharth once walked out over, but also caring, not angry.

qa.q: Why was a private letter wiser than joining Kunal's teasing?
qa.a: It lets Siddharth explain, or say nothing is wrong, without the group watching, so the friendship stays safe either way.

qa.q: How might Siddharth feel reading this compared with hearing the teasing at the party?
qa.a: Siddharth may feel relieved and less cornered by a quiet letter, though perhaps a little embarrassed that the change was noticed.

grounding: Illustrates a friend who notices someone laughing along with jokes they used to dislike and reaches out privately and kindly instead of teasing in front of the group.
